Definition: from G303 (in the sense of reversal) and a derivative of G4632; properly, to pack up (baggage), i.e. (by implication, and figuratively) to upset:--subvert.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the letter from the Jerusalem council: 'Forasmuch as we have heard, that certain which went out from us have troubled you with words, subverting your souls, saying, Ye must be circumcised, and keep the law: to whom we gave no such commandment.' It means to pack up and upset — to turn a soul upside down — and the council says plainly that the men who did it had no authority from them.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for subverting carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the letter — the council disowning the men who troubled the Gentiles with a law they never gave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
